concepts.label: MNCs and Production Across Countries
concepts.cardText: Until the middle of the twentieth century, production was largely organised within countries, and trade was the main channel connecting them. A multinational corporation (MNC) is a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation. MNCs set up offices and factories where they can get cheap labour and other resources, so that the cost of production is low and they earn greater profits. For example, an MNC may design products in the US, make components in China, assemble them in Mexico and Eastern Europe, and run customer care from call centres in India. The production process is divided into small parts and spread across the globe.
concepts.hint: Why would one company design in the US, manufacture in China and run call centres in India?
concepts.probe: What is an MNC, and why do MNCs spread their production across countries?
concepts.causeChain: MNCs seek cheap labour and other resources -> cost of production falls -> greater profits -> production divided into small parts and spread across countries

causeLinks.criterion: Connects MNCs seeking cheap labour and resources (to lower costs and earn more profit) to their spreading production across countries.

keyPoints.text: Until the middle of the twentieth century, production was largely organised within countries. What crossed the boundaries were raw material, food stuff and finished products. Trade was the main channel connecting distant countries.

checks.criterion: States that until the mid-twentieth century production was organised within countries and trade was the main channel connecting them.

keyPoints.text: A MNC is a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation. MNCs set up offices and factories for production in regions where they can get cheap labour and other resources. This is done so that the cost of production is low and the MNCs can earn greater profits.

keyPoints.text: The MNC is not only selling its finished products globally, but the goods and services are produced globally. The production process is divided into small parts and spread out across the globe. China provides a cheap manufacturing location; Mexico and Eastern Europe are close to markets in the US and Europe; India has highly skilled engineers and educated English-speaking youth for customer care.

concepts.label: How MNCs Interlink Production
concepts.cardText: MNCs set up production close to markets, where labour is available at low cost and other factors of production are assured. Money spent on assets like land, buildings and machines is investment; investment by MNCs is foreign investment. MNCs may set up production jointly with local companies, bringing money and the latest technology. The most common route is to buy up local companies, as Cargill Foods bought Parakh Foods. MNCs also place orders with small producers, in garments, footwear and sports items, and sell under their own brands, with great power over price, quality, delivery and labour conditions. As a result, production in distant locations is getting interlinked.
concepts.hint: Think of three routes: partnering with local companies, buying them, and ordering from small producers.
concepts.probe: What are the various ways in which MNCs set up, control or produce in other countries?
concepts.causeChain: MNCs invest (foreign investment) through joint production, buying local companies, or orders to small producers -> strong influence on production in distant places -> production across countries gets interlinked

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the ways MNCs work with local producers (partnering, buying, placing orders) to production in distant locations becoming interlinked.

keyPoints.text: In general, MNCs set up production where it is close to the markets; where there is skilled and unskilled labour available at low costs; and where the availability of other factors of production is assured. MNCs might also look for government policies that look after their interests.

checks.criterion: Explains where MNCs set up production: close to markets, with low-cost skilled and unskilled labour, assured factors of production, or favourable government policies.

keyPoints.text: The money that is spent to buy assets such as land, building, machines and other equipment is called investment. Investment made by MNCs is called foreign investment. Any investment is made with the hope that these assets will earn profits.
keyPoints.followUp: What is meant by investment, and what is it called when MNCs make it?

checks.criterion: Defines investment as money spent to buy assets such as land, buildings and machines, and foreign investment as investment made by MNCs.

keyPoints.text: At times, MNCs set up production jointly with local companies. The benefit to the local company is two-fold: MNCs can provide money for additional investments like new machines, and might bring the latest technology. But the most common route for MNC investments is to buy up local companies and then to expand production; for example Cargill Foods, a very large American MNC, bought Parakh Foods and is now the largest producer of edible oil in India.

checks.criterion: Explains joint production with local companies, where MNCs provide money for investment and the latest technology.

The products are supplied to the MNCs, which sell them under their own brand names. These large MNCs have tremendous power to determine price, quality, delivery, and labour conditions for these distant producers. As a result, production in these widely dispersed locations is getting interlinked.

topics.title: Foreign trade and integration of markets

concepts.label: Foreign Trade and Integration of Markets
concepts.cardText: Foreign trade creates an opportunity for producers to reach beyond domestic markets, and for buyers to choose goods beyond what is produced at home. When Chinese toy makers export cheaper, new-design toys to India, 70 to 80 per cent of toy shops replace Indian toys within a year: Indian buyers get more choice at lower prices and Chinese makers expand, but Indian toy makers face losses. With trade, the choice of goods rises, prices of similar goods in the two markets tend to become equal, and producers in distant countries compete closely. Foreign trade thus integrates markets in different countries.
concepts.hint: What happened to toy prices, buyers and Indian toy makers when Chinese toys arrived?
concepts.probe: How does foreign trade lead to integration of markets across countries? Explain with an example.
concepts.causeChain: Foreign trade lets goods travel between markets -> more choice, prices of similar goods become equal, producers compete closely -> markets in different countries get integrated

causeLinks.criterion: Connects goods travelling between markets (more choice, equal prices, close competition) to the integration of markets in different countries.

keyPoints.text: Foreign trade creates an opportunity for the producers to reach beyond the domestic markets, i.e., markets of their own countries. Producers can also compete in markets in other countries. Similarly, for the buyers, import of goods produced in another country is one way of expanding the choice of goods beyond what is domestically produced.
keyPoints.followUp: How does foreign trade help producers and buyers?

checks.criterion: Explains that foreign trade lets producers reach markets beyond their own country and expands buyers' choice beyond domestic goods.

keyPoints.text: Chinese manufacturers export plastic toys to India. Because of cheaper prices and new designs, within a year 70 to 80 per cent of the toy shops have replaced Indian toys with Chinese toys. Indian buyers have a greater choice of toys and at lower prices; Chinese toy makers expand business; Indian toy makers face losses, as their toys are selling much less.
keyPoints.followUp: What happened in India when toys from China came into the market?

checks.criterion: Uses the Chinese toys example: Indian buyers get more choice at lower prices, while Indian toy makers face losses.

keyPoints.text: In general, with the opening of trade, goods travel from one market to another. Choice of goods in the markets rises. Prices of similar goods in the two markets tend to become equal. And, producers in the two countries now closely compete against each other even though they are separated by thousands of miles. Foreign trade thus results in connecting the markets or integration of markets in different countries.
keyPoints.followUp: What happens to choice and prices in two markets once trade opens between them?

checks.criterion: Names the effects of opening trade: choice of goods rises, prices of similar goods tend to become equal, and producers in different countries compete closely.
States that foreign trade results in the integration of markets in different countries.

acceptedExamples: Chinese toys replacing Indian toys in 70 to 80 per cent of toy shops
Trade routes connecting India to markets in the East and West; the East India Company

concepts.label: What Is Globalisation?
concepts.cardText: In the past two to three decades, more MNCs have looked for cheap locations, so foreign investment has been rising, and foreign trade has risen rapidly, with a large part controlled by MNCs. The result of greater foreign investment and greater foreign trade has been greater integration of production and markets across countries. Globalisation is this process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries, and MNCs are playing a major role in it. Goods, services, investments and technology move between countries, but movement of people has not increased much because of restrictions.

concepts.label: Technology and Globalisation
concepts.cardText: Rapid improvement in technology has been one major factor stimulating globalisation. Transport technology has made faster delivery of goods over long distances possible at lower costs: goods are placed in containers loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks, hugely reducing port handling costs, and air transport costs have fallen. Information and communication technology (telecommunications, computers, the Internet) has played a major role in spreading production of services across countries. For example, a news magazine for London readers is designed and printed in Delhi, with text, instructions and payment sent over the Internet.
concepts.hint: How do containers and the Internet make it cheaper to produce in one country and sell in another?
concepts.probe: How has technology, especially IT, helped the process of globalisation?
concepts.causeChain: Better transport technology (containers, cheaper air transport) -> faster, cheaper delivery of goods; IT (telecom, computers, Internet) -> services produced in one country for another -> globalisation stimulated

causeLinks.criterion: Connects information and communication technology to the spreading of production of services across countries (for example a London magazine designed in Delhi).

checks.criterion: States that rapid improvement in technology has been a major factor stimulating globalisation.

concepts.label: Liberalisation of Foreign Trade and Investment
concepts.cardText: A tax on imports, like a tax on imported toys, is a trade barrier: a restriction governments use to regulate foreign trade. After Independence, India put barriers on foreign trade and investment to protect producers from foreign competition, since industries were just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s; only essential items like machinery, fertilisers and petroleum were imported. Around 1991, India decided its producers should compete globally, as competition would improve their performance and quality; this was supported by powerful international organisations. Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is called liberalisation.
concepts.hint: Why did India protect its industries after Independence, and why did it remove the barriers around 1991?
concepts.probe: Why did the Indian government put barriers on foreign trade and investment, and why did it remove them?
concepts.causeChain: Young industries in the 1950s-60s -> trade barriers to protect them from foreign competition; around 1991 -> belief that competition would improve quality -> barriers removed (liberalisation) -> goods and foreign companies come in more easily

causeLinks.criterion: Contrasts why barriers were put up (to protect young industries from competition) with why they were removed (competition would improve producers' performance and quality).

keyPoints.text: Tax on imports is an example of trade barrier. It is called a barrier because some restriction has been set up. Governments can use trade barriers to increase or decrease (regulate) foreign trade and decide what kinds of goods, and how much of each, should come into the country. A limit on the number of goods that can be imported is known as quotas.

checks.criterion: Explains a trade barrier as a restriction on foreign trade, such as a tax on imports or a quota, used by governments to regulate trade.

keyPoints.text: The Indian government, after Independence, had put barriers to foreign trade and foreign investment. This was considered necessary to protect the producers within the country from foreign competition. Industries were just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s, and competition from imports would not have allowed them to come up. India allowed imports of only essential items such as machinery, fertilisers, petroleum.
keyPoints.followUp: Why did India put barriers on foreign trade and investment after Independence?

checks.criterion: Explains that after Independence India put up trade barriers to protect producers from foreign competition, because industries were just coming up.

keyPoints.text: Starting around 1991, far-reaching changes in policy were made. The government decided that Indian producers should compete with producers around the globe, feeling that competition would improve their performance since they would have to improve their quality. This decision was supported by powerful international organisations. Barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment were removed to a large extent.
keyPoints.followUp: What changed in India's policy around 1991, and why?

checks.criterion: Explains that around 1991 barriers were removed because the government felt competition would improve producers' performance and quality.

keyPoints.text: Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is what is known as liberalisation. With liberalisation of trade, businesses are allowed to make decisions freely about what they wish to import or export.
keyPoints.followUp: What does liberalisation mean?

checks.criterion: Defines liberalisation as removing barriers or restrictions set by the government, letting businesses decide freely what to import or export.

acceptedExamples: A tax on imported Chinese toys as a trade barrier

concepts.label: World Trade Organisation
concepts.cardText: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) aims to liberalise international trade. Started at the initiative of developed countries, it establishes rules for international trade and sees that they are obeyed; about 160 countries are members. In practice, developed countries have unfairly retained trade barriers, while WTO rules have forced developing countries to remove them. For example, US farmers, only 0.5 per cent of US employment, receive massive government support, so they sell farm products abroad at abnormally low prices, hurting farmers in other countries. Developing countries ask: is this free and fair trade?
concepts.hint: Who started the WTO? Do all countries follow its rules equally?

concepts.causeChain: WTO (started by developed countries) makes trade rules -> developing countries forced to remove barriers -> developed countries keep supporting their farmers -> cheap subsidised exports hurt farmers elsewhere -> trade not free and fair

causeLinks.criterion: Connects developed countries like the US giving massive support to their farmers to trade under the WTO not being fair for developing countries.

keyPoints.text: World Trade Organisation (WTO) is one such organisation whose aim is to liberalise international trade. concepts.label: Who Has Benefited from Globalisation?
concepts.cardText: Greater competition among local and foreign producers has benefited consumers, particularly the well-off in urban areas, who enjoy more choice, better quality and lower prices, and so higher standards of living. But among producers and workers, the impact has not been uniform. MNCs have increased investment in India in cell phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food and banking, creating new jobs and helping local suppliers. Several top Indian companies have benefited by investing in newer technology, and some, like Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints and Sundaram Fasteners, have become multinationals. New opportunities have opened in IT-based services.

keyPoints.text: Globalisation and greater competition among producers, both local and foreign, has been of advantage to consumers, particularly the well-off sections in the urban areas. There is greater choice before these consumers who now enjoy improved quality and lower prices for several products, and much higher standards of living than earlier.

concepts.label: Steps to Attract Foreign Investment
concepts.cardText: Central and state governments take special steps to attract foreign companies. Special Economic Zones (SEZs) are set up with world-class facilities like electricity, water, roads, transport and storage, and companies there pay no taxes for an initial period of five years. The government has also allowed flexibility in labour laws: instead of hiring workers regularly, companies hire them 'flexibly' for short periods when work is intense, to reduce labour costs. Foreign companies are demanding even more flexibility.
concepts.hint: What do SEZs offer companies? What does 'flexible' hiring mean for workers?
concepts.probe: What steps has the government taken to attract foreign investment, and how does flexibility in labour laws help companies?
concepts.causeChain: Government wants foreign investment -> SEZs with world-class facilities and five years without taxes + flexible labour laws -> lower costs for companies -> more foreign investment, but less job security for workers

causeLinks.criterion: Connects flexible labour laws and SEZ incentives to lower costs for companies, which attracts foreign investment.

keyPoints.text: The central and state governments in India are taking special steps to attract foreign companies. Industrial zones called Special Economic Zones (SEZs) are being set up, with world class facilities: electricity, water, roads, transport, storage, recreational and educational facilities. Companies in SEZs do not have to pay taxes for an initial period of five years.
keyPoints.followUp: What special zones has the government set up to attract foreign companies, and what do they offer?

checks.criterion: Explains Special Economic Zones: world-class facilities, and no taxes for an initial period of five years.

keyPoints.text: Government has also allowed flexibility in the labour laws to attract foreign investment. Instead of hiring workers on a regular basis, companies hire workers 'flexibly' for short periods when there is intense pressure of work. This is done to reduce the cost of labour for the company. Foreign companies are demanding more flexibility in labour laws.
keyPoints.followUp: How have labour laws been changed to attract foreign investment?

checks.criterion: Explains flexibility in labour laws: companies hire workers flexibly for short periods instead of regularly, to reduce labour costs.

acceptedExamples: Exercise: 'How would flexibility in labour laws help companies?'
Exercise: 'Why do governments try to attract more foreign investment?'

concepts.label: Small Producers: Compete or Perish
concepts.cardText: For many small producers and workers, globalisation has posed major challenges. Ravi started a capacitor unit in Hosur in 1992; his struggle began when the government removed restrictions on imports of capacitors under its WTO agreement in 2001. Television companies moved to assembling for MNCs and preferred imports at half his price. Ravi now produces less than half of what he did in 2000 and has only seven workers. Batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products and vegetable oil are industries where small manufacturers have been hit hard. Small and medium industries employ about 11 crore workers, next only to agriculture.
concepts.hint: What happened to Ravi's capacitor business after import restrictions were removed in 2001?
concepts.probe: How has rising competition from globalisation affected small producers in India?
concepts.causeChain: Import restrictions removed (WTO agreement, 2001) -> cheaper imports and MNC competition -> small producers like Ravi lose customers -> output falls, units close, workers lose jobs

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the removal of import restrictions and cheaper imports to small producers losing business and closing units.

keyPoints.text: For a large number of small producers and workers globalisation has posed major challenges. Ravi's struggle to run his capacitor company started when the government removed restrictions on imports of capacitors as per its agreement at WTO in 2001. His clients, television companies, preferred imports at half his price. Ravi now produces less than half the capacitors he produced in 2000 and has only seven workers.
keyPoints.followUp: What happened to Ravi's capacitor company, and why?

checks.criterion: Explains how small producers like Ravi were hurt when import restrictions were removed (WTO agreement, 2001) and cheaper imports took their customers.

keyPoints.text: Batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products, and vegetable oil are some examples of industries where the small manufacturers have been hit hard due to competition. Several units have shut down, rendering many workers jobless. The small and medium industries in India employ the largest number of workers (11 crores) in the country, next only to agriculture.
keyPoints.followUp: Which small industries have been hit by competition, and what happened to their workers?

checks.criterion: States that small manufacturers in industries like batteries, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy or vegetable oil have been hit hard, with units shutting down and workers losing jobs.
Mentions that small and medium industries employ about 11 crore workers, next only to agriculture.

keyPoints.text: Recent studies point out that small producers in India need three things to compete better: better roads, power, water, raw materials, marketing and information network; improvement and modernisation of technology; and timely availability of credit at reasonable interest rates.

checks.criterion: Names what small producers need to compete: better infrastructure, modernised technology, or timely credit at reasonable rates.

acceptedExamples: Ravi's capacitor unit in Hosur, Tamil Nadu

concepts.label: Competition and Uncertain Employment
concepts.cardText: Faced with growing competition, most employers now prefer to employ workers 'flexibly', so workers' jobs are no longer secure. Large garment MNCs in Europe and America look for the cheapest goods; to win orders, Indian exporters cut labour costs by hiring temporary workers, with long hours, night shifts and low wages. Sushila, once a permanent garment worker with health insurance and provident fund, is now a temporary worker earning less than half as much, with no benefits. While MNCs make large profits, workers are denied their fair share of the benefits of globalisation. Conditions in the organised sector have come to resemble the unorganised sector.
concepts.hint: Why would exporters hire workers only temporarily? What happened to Sushila?
concepts.probe: How has competition affected workers in industries like garment exports?
concepts.causeChain: MNCs look for the cheapest goods -> exporters compete for orders by cutting labour costs -> temporary jobs, long hours, low wages, no benefits -> workers denied a fair share; organised sector conditions resemble the unorganised sector

causeLinks.criterion: Connects growing competition among exporters to cutting labour costs through temporary, insecure and low-paid jobs.

keyPoints.text: Globalisation and the pressure of competition have substantially changed the lives of workers. Faced with growing competition, most employers these days prefer to employ workers 'flexibly'. This means that workers' jobs are no longer secure.
keyPoints.followUp: How have employers changed the way they hire workers because of competition?

checks.criterion: States that because of competition, employers prefer to employ workers flexibly, so workers' jobs are no longer secure.

keyPoints.text: Large garment MNCs look for the cheapest goods to maximise profits. To get large orders, Indian garment exporters cut labour costs: they employ workers only on a temporary basis, with very long working hours and night shifts in peak season, at low wages. While this competition has allowed the MNCs to make large profits, workers are denied their fair share of benefits brought about by globalisation.
keyPoints.followUp: How do garment exporters keep their costs low, and what does it mean for workers?

checks.criterion: Explains that garment exporters cut labour costs by hiring temporary workers with long hours and low wages, so workers are denied their fair share of benefits.
Gives the example of Sushila, who lost her permanent job and benefits and now works as a temporary worker for less than half her earlier wage.

keyPoints.text: Most workers today are employed in the unorganised sector. Moreover, increasingly conditions of work in the organised sector have come to resemble the unorganised sector. Workers in the organised sector such as Sushila no longer get the protection and benefits that they enjoyed earlier.

checks.criterion: States that conditions in the organised sector have come to resemble the unorganised sector; workers no longer get earlier protection and benefits.

acceptedExamples: Sushila, a garment export worker in Delhi

topics.title: The struggle for a fair globalisation

concepts.label: The Struggle for a Fair Globalisation
concepts.cardText: Not everyone has benefited from globalisation: people with education, skill and wealth have made the best use of the new opportunities, while many have not shared the benefits. Fair globalisation would create opportunities for all and ensure that its benefits are shared better. The government can play a major role: ensuring labour laws are properly implemented and workers get their rights, supporting small producers until they can compete, using trade and investment barriers if necessary, negotiating at the WTO for 'fairer rules', and aligning with other developing countries. Campaigns by people's organisations have also influenced decisions at the WTO.
concepts.hint: What can the government and ordinary people do so that more people share the benefits of globalisation?
concepts.probe: What is fair globalisation, and how can the government and people help achieve it?
concepts.causeChain: Benefits of globalisation not shared equally (educated, skilled, wealthy gain most) -> need for fair globalisation -> government protects workers and small producers, negotiates fairer WTO rules; people's campaigns influence decisions

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the unequal sharing of globalisation's benefits to the need for fair globalisation that creates opportunities for all.

keyPoints.text: Not everyone has benefited from globalisation. People with education, skill and wealth have made the best use of the new opportunities. On the other hand, there are many people who have not shared the benefits.
keyPoints.followUp: Has everyone benefited from globalisation? Who has gained the most?

checks.criterion: States that not everyone has benefited: people with education, skill and wealth used the new opportunities best, while many have not shared the benefits.

keyPoints.text: Fair globalisation would create opportunities for all, and also ensure that the benefits of globalisation are shared better.
keyPoints.followUp: What would fair globalisation look like?

checks.criterion: Explains that fair globalisation would create opportunities for all and ensure its benefits are shared better.

keyPoints.text: The government can play a major role. It can ensure that labour laws are properly implemented and the workers get their rights. It can support small producers to improve their performance till they become strong enough to compete. If necessary, it can use trade and investment barriers. It can negotiate at the WTO for 'fairer rules' and align with other developing countries against the domination of developed countries in the WTO.
keyPoints.followUp: What can the government do to make globalisation fairer?

checks.criterion: Suggests the government ensure labour laws are properly implemented and workers get their rights.
Suggests the government support small producers until they are strong enough to compete, using trade and investment barriers if necessary.
Suggests the government negotiate at the WTO for fairer rules, aligning with other developing countries.

keyPoints.text: In the past few years, massive campaigns and representation by people's organisations have influenced important decisions relating to trade and investments at the WTO. This has demonstrated that people also can play an important role in the struggle for fair globalisation.

checks.criterion: Mentions that campaigns by people's organisations have influenced WTO decisions, showing people can help achieve fair globalisation.

acceptedExamples: A demonstration against the WTO in Hong Kong, 2005
